prs.title: turbopack: experimental minify-before-chunking feature
prs.author: andrewimm
prs.body:
Minification happens on a per-chunk basis. With enough chunks, we get good parallelization, but a large chunk can create a single large span that wastes unused cores.
This flag makes minification more granular, applying it to each module and caching the result. The goal is to make each minification step smaller, so that they can be evenly distributed across parallel workers. Theoretically this may also reduce the work done on a re-build, since the minification transform will only be applied to changed modules.

The flag is configured behind an `experimental` config flag, and only applies to builds (because we don't minify in dev!).

An ideal outcome is equal-or-faster builds, with almost no change to byte size. I don't expect much change to byte size, becuase the shape of our chunks doesn't lend itself to cross-module optimizations, but it's entirely possible we regress this a bit. That hypothesis will need to be tested against our benchmark suite of real Next apps.

---

## How it works

`experimental.turbopackMinifyBeforeChunking` sets `minify_before_chunking` on the browser and Node.js chunking contexts (Next.js client, server and edge). The chunk content then picks one of three modes (`ChunkMinification`): no minification, whole-chunk (today's behavior), or per-item.

**Per-item minification** (`minify_chunk_item` in `turbopack-ecmascript/src/minify.rs`):
- Each module factory is minified on its own, in a cached task keyed by that factory, so a rebuild only re-minifies ch
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbo-tasks: add batched keyed reads via KeyedReadRef
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds `vc.keyed_reader().await?`, which returns a `KeyedReadRef<T>` for `cell = "keyed"` values, and uses it for NFT generation (`crates/next-api/src/nft.rs`, `crates/next-api/src/nft_json.rs`).

### Why

`vc.get(key).await?` and `vc.contains_key(key).await?` register a fine-grained dependency per read. Every read is a separate future that takes backend locks to register its dependency. That gets expensive when one task reads many keys from the same map, as the NFT tasks do.

### How

- **API:** `keyed_reader()` returns a `ReadKeyedReaderVcFuture<T>` resolving to `Result<KeyedReadRef<T>>`. It reads the cell once. The `KeyedReadRef` only allows synchronous `get(key)` and `contains_key(key)` calls. It records the hashes of the accessed keys (the same hash `vc.get` uses), not the keys themselves.
- **Dependency while alive:** calling `keyed_reader()` allocates a dedicated `CellKey::Keyed(id)` dependency for the current task execution before the future is created. `id` is unique within that execution. For invalidation it behaves like a full-cell dependency, but as a separate entry it can be removed without affecting normal full reads of the same cell or other `KeyedReadRef`s. A call outside a task execution is a normal full-dependency read.
- **Dropped within the same execution:** one batched backend call replaces the `Keyed(id)` dependency with `CellKey::Hash(h)` dependencies for the accessed keys. Like `vc.get`, the reader is then only invalidated when one of those k
…(truncated)

The serializer now omits these entries, following the fix proposed by @ahmedgabrrr in PR #101004. The regression tests cover tag revalidation before and after path revalidation, plus repeated timed revalidation.

We're using a branch in `vercel/next.js` so the new tests can run in deploy CI, which is unavailable for fork PRs.

prs.title: [no-unsafe-inline] Add an experimental flag for React's external browser runtime
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
React's Fizz streams its instruction set as inline `<script>` tags, which forces a Content-Security-Policy to allow `unsafe-inline` unless a per-response nonce is used, and a per-response nonce is incompatible with static generation. This change adds `experimental.externalBrowserRuntime`, which switches Fizz to React's `unstable_server-external-runtime` so the instructions are emitted as `<template data-rci>` elements and applied in the browser by a standalone runtime script instead. Since React only ships that runtime on its experimental channel, enabling the flag opts the `app` directory into `react@experimental` alongside `taint`, `blockingSSR`, `transitionIndicator`, and `gestureTransition`.

The visible consequence is one additional static asset under `/_next/static/chunks` and one additional `<script>` tag in the document head. Next.js adds neither of them: React emits the tag itself once `unstable_externalRuntimeSrc` is set, marked `async` and carrying the nonce and integrity. In exchange React stops injecting its inline form-replaying runtime, since the external runtime covers it.

This is App Router only; the Pages Router still inlines React's instructions. It is also one step in a larger effort to let applications drop `unsafe-inline` entirely. The Flight payload and `bootstrapScriptContent` are still emitted as inline scripts, and moving them onto the same mechanism will be gated behind this same feature flag.

prs.title: Add router.experimental_prepare()
prs.author: acdlite
prs.body:
Adds `experimental_prepare(href)` to the router returned by `useRouter()`. It starts a navigation that goes through all the same steps as a regular one, including the dynamic request, but doesn't update the router. The response writes into the same local cache used by back/forward navigations.

The returned handle has `push()` and `replace()`. Committing performs a regular navigation, except it can read bfcache entries written since the prepare began, regardless of stale time. If the prepared request is still in flight, the commit reuses it instead of starting a new one.

The intended use is to prepare on pointerdown and commit on click, which starts the dynamic request earlier. We may build this into Link eventually; the low-level API lets people try it out first.

Semantics:

- If you don't commit, nothing else happens. The data stays in the bfcache, so a history traversal to an overlapping segment may observe it. This is intentional. The contract of the API is that you are OK with the navigation showing data that's as stale as when the preparation began.
- Prepared data doesn't expire. Committing much later still reuses it; the caller is responsible for not holding on to a handle too long.
- A refresh or server action between prepare and commit invalidates the prepared data, the same way it invalidates the bfcache.
- A handle can only be committed once. Later calls are a no-op, with a dev-only warning.
- A regular navigation to the same route doesn't reuse prepared data; o
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(turbopack): invalidate lazy compilation state across sessions
prs.author: fireairforce
prs.body:
### What?

Fix lazy compilation state invalidation after restoring the Turbopack filesystem cache.

Related: https://github.com/utooland/utoo/issues/3367

### Why?

`LazyCompilationState` is not serialized and is recreated in each session. However, tasks that previously read it can restore cached results without subscribing to the new state's invalidation list.

As a result, activating a lazy import after a restart can succeed while cached readers still report it as inactive.

### How?

Mark `lazy_compilation_state` as `session_dependent` so dependent tasks recompute and subscribe to the recreated state.

Add a Rust regression test covering three sessions sharing the same persistent cache, including:
- Activating an import whose inactive state was previously cached.
- Reactivating an import in a subsequent session.
- Reading before activation and activating before reading.

### Verification

- The regression test fails before the fix and passes afterward.
- All 9 existing lazy dynamic import browser tests pass.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings --no-deps` pass.

prs.title: Pin Tailwind to 4.3.3 in create-next-app
prs.author: jamiboym
prs.body:
## Summary

New `create-next-app` projects that use Tailwind currently fail to build on Node.js versions that can't `require()` ES modules: before 20.19, and 22.0–22.11. That range includes Next.js's minimum supported version, 20.9.0:

```
./app/globals.css
Error: require() of ES Module …/node_modules/magic-string/dist/index.mjs not supported.
    at …/node_modules/@tailwindcss/node/dist/index.js
    at …/node_modules/@tailwindcss/turbopack/dist/index.js
```

`@tailwindcss/node@4.3.4`, published 2026-11-02 at 21:36 UTC, moved from `magic-string@^0.30.21` to `magic-string@^1.1.0`. magic-string 1.x is ESM-only, but Tailwind's CommonJS build still `require()`s it. The template's `^4` ranges pick up the new version. Since then, every Tailwind create-next-app test in the Node 20.9.0 jobs has failed on canary and on the PR runs checked: turbopack production, turbopack dev and cache components dev. That includes the run that blamed f699e1093d.

This temporarily pins `tailwindcss` and the Tailwind bundler plugin (`@tailwindcss/turbopack` or `@tailwindcss/postcss`) to `4.3.3`. That version's `@tailwindcss/node` still depends on `magic-string@^0.30.21`. Restore `^4` once Tailwind ships a fix.

## Verification

- Reproduced the failure locally: on Node 20.20.2 with `--no-experimental-require-module`, `require()` of a package shaped like `magic-string@1.4.5` throws the same `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`.
- Not run locally: the create-next-app tests, because the sandbox can't reach the npm registry. 
…(truncated)

prs.title: Fix layout client chunk leakage across async server imports
prs.author: mischnic
prs.body:
## Summary

When a layout reaches a shared client reference through a server-side `import()`, the reference can belong to different chunk groups than its owner. Falling back to every group containing that reference could then pull unrelated page code into the layout’s initial client chunks.

Select groups by direct owner membership or transitive async-import ancestry, with cycle detection. Only fall back when owner information is absent; error when a known owner cannot be matched.

Fixes #100893.

## Verification

Added async/nested/cyclic regression coverage. Existing layout chunk-sharing and CSS-order tests pass in production and development with rebuilt native bindings.

prs.title: Turbopack: use simd-utf16-len for source position column counting
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #100919. `SourcePos::update` now counts the UTF-16 length of the final line segment with the SIMD kernels of [`simd-utf16-len`](https://github.com/SyMind/simd-utf16-len), so that counting is fast even on long lines such as minified code.

It uses `utf16_len_bytes`, the safe byte-slice API added in `simd-utf16-len` 0.4.0 (https://github.com/SyMind/simd-utf16-len/pull/22). `SourcePos::update` passes rope bytes directly, with no `unsafe` conversion to `&str`. The result is exact for valid UTF-8. For other bytes the call is still safe, but the count is unspecified.

Line-terminator handling and the complete-text chunk contract from #100919 are unchanged. The `SourcePos` tests continue to cover column semantics.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p turbopack-core --lib`
- `cargo fmt -p turbopack-core --check`
- `cargo clippy -p turbopack-core --tests`

prs.title: turbo-tasks: add cancelable cell reads via Vc::lazy_reader()
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Adds `vc.lazy_reader().await?`, which returns a `LazyReadRef<T>` for any value type: a cell read that can be canceled. The value is only accessible through an explicit `LazyReadRef::get()`.

- While the ref is alive, the task depends on the whole cell, so invalidations during the execution are not lost.
- If the ref is dropped without `get()` ever being called, the read is canceled: the task no longer depends on the cell through it.
- If `get()` was called, the read behaves like a normal `.await`.

Built on the per-execution provisional dependency machinery from #100884 (`keyed_reader()`), whose `CellKey::Keyed(id)` this PR renames to `CellKey::Provisional(id)`.

### Why?

Some tasks need a cell's value only in rare cases, and only find out in synchronous code. One example is the server actions hash salt (encryption key) in #100950. Today that needs an optimistic "run without it, bail, re-run with it" strategy. With `lazy_reader()`, the task can read the cell up front, pass the ref into synchronous code, and depend on it only when it is actually used.

### How?

- **API:** `Vc::lazy_reader()` returns a named `ReadLazyReaderVcFuture<T>`, mirroring `Vc::keyed_reader()` / `ReadKeyedReaderVcFuture<T>`.
  - Both futures share one `CancelableDependencyRead`, extracted from the `keyed_reader()` future.
  - On creation it allocates a per-execution `CellKey::Provisional(id)` dependency (a temporary hold on the whole cell) and registers it as alive.
  - On success it hands t
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: avoid invalidating per-module analysis when the encryption key changes
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Changing the server actions encryption key between two warm Turbopack builds no longer re-runs per-module analysis (parsing, export analysis, reference resolution).

Uses `lazy_reader()` from #101008.

### Why?

The key changes in three situations:

- `encryption-utils-server.ts` rotates it during builds, after 14 days.
- Users set a different `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` per build.
- On lts, it changed on every build in Docker (fixed on canary by #100790).

A key change invalidated almost the whole build graph, for two reasons:

1. `Project` stored `encryption_key` and `build_id` as plain fields, so every task reading `Project` was invalidated when either changed.
2. The server actions transform runs on every JS module and read the key (the salt for server reference IDs) for **all** of them. So every module parse depended on the key, even though only modules containing `"use server"` / `"use cache"` generate IDs.

### How?

- **Isolate the values.** `encryption_key` and `build_id` now live in their own cells on `Project`, following the `preview_props` pattern from #100425. The `Project` value stays equal when only these values change. Only the tasks that actually read them are invalidated: `edge_env`, and the server actions transform for modules that generate IDs.
- **Read the salt lazily.**
  - `Config::hash_salt` is now a small `HashSalt` type in `next-custom-transforms`. It holds either a value or a lazy getter, and the transform only reads it when it g
…(truncated)

prs.title: Fix blocking revalidation for `fetch` and `unstable_cache`
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
> [!TIP]
> This PR is best reviewed with whitespace changes hidden.

With Cache Components enabled, a page that uses cached `fetch` calls or `unstable_cache` can return a 500 during on-demand revalidation, including blocking regeneration after `expire`. Both wrappers skip the incremental cache lookup, so the final prerender cannot reuse the data computed by the prospective pass. It repeats asynchronous work and fails with `NEXT_STATIC_GEN_BAILOUT`.

The incremental cache now reads the Resume Data Cache (RDC) during on-demand revalidation before it bypasses persisted entries. Both `unstable_cache` and cached `fetch` calls use this path, so the final prerender can reuse the prospective pass's result.

This extends the fix proposed in PR #100895 to cached fetches and preserves the forced-refresh behavior introduced in PR #48516. The incremental cache continues to apply its tag invalidation checks before it returns an entry.

Fixes #99866
Closes #100895

prs.title: [experiment] [turbopack-cli] compile .go files
prs.author: timneutkens
prs.body:
## Summary

Add experimental Go file compilation to Turbopack and its CLI. Go owns package discovery, compilation, and linking; Turbopack tracks the reported sources, modules, embedded assets, assembly, and headers, then emits an executable through the normal output pipeline.

The reusable compiler APIs support generated-source overlays, persistent executable caching, tracked source selection, cached top-level declaration analysis, and host/target sessions. Analysis and compilation share source identity and publication validity checks. Session ownership handles lazy toolchain probing, cancellation, and shared module-cache watcher leases.

The CLI supports explicit same-directory Go files, mixed Go and JavaScript entries, build/watch/dev, and offline dependencies prepared in the module cache. With `--persistent-caching`, Go-only and mixed builds restore compiler output across CLI processes while JavaScript tasks retain their independent persistent identity. Watchers and cancellation belong to the current process, including after a warm restore. Framework consumers can generate their own entrypoints without implementing Go parsing or compiler lifecycle. Application routing, runtime execution, output naming, and manifests remain consumer-owned. The route-handler integration is in #100130.

## Verification

- Rust clippy passed for `turbopack-go`, `next-api`, and `next-napi-bindings` with warnings denied.

- Go compiler: unit tests and ten live tests passed, including source edit
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: keep CSS Modules when a loader rule's `as` adds an existing extension
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

A Turbopack loader rule like the one `create-next-app` generates for Tailwind CSS:

```js
turbopack: {
  rules: {
    '*.css': { loaders: ['@tailwindcss/turbopack'], as: '*.css' },
  },
},
```

broke CSS Modules without any warning. Every `*.module.css` import came back as `{}`, and the module's selectors were emitted unscoped as global CSS. This happens with a pass-through loader too, and still happens on current canary.

**Why:** `as` replaces `*` with the full file path, so the loader output for `page.module.css` was renamed to `page.module.css.css`. That name no longer ends in `.module.css`, so the CSS Module's inner and analyze references were reprocessed as global CSS, which exports no classes.

**Fix:** when a loader's `as` pattern is a single leading `*` followed by a suffix the file name already ends with (e.g. `*.css` on `foo.css` / `foo.module.css`), Turbopack now keeps the original file name. Such a rule then behaves exactly like one without `as`, which already worked. The check lives in `WebpackLoadersProcessedAsset::ident`, so it covers both `turbopack.rules` and the `turbopackAs` import attribute. `AssetIdent::rename_as` and renames that change the extension (`*.svg` → `*.js`, `*.module.scss` → `*.module.css`, …) are unchanged.

Fixes #100548
Finding: https://next-maintainer-agent.vercel.tools/agent-feedback/5921

### Places that state or depend on this behavior

- `docs/01-app/03-api-reference/05-config/01-next-config-js/turbopack.mdx`: added a not
…(truncated)

prs.title: perf(build): use nft's cached readlink when collecting build traces
prs.author: shootaroo
prs.body:
### What?

Use nft's built-in cached `readlink` in `collect-build-traces.ts`.

### Why?

- Since #56817, a custom `readlink` is passed to `nodeFileTrace`. Unlike nft's built-in one, it isn't cached, so every call goes to the filesystem.
- nft's `realpath` walks up all parent directories again for every path it resolves, so with pnpm's deep `node_modules/.pnpm/...` layout these calls pile up.
  - In our app, `readlink` was called about 479k times for only about 9,100 distinct paths.
- nft's built-in `readlink` also [returns `null` for the same error codes (`EINVAL` / `ENOENT` / `UNKNOWN`)](https://github.com/vercel/nft/blob/1.10.2/src/fs.ts#L72-L84), so removing it doesn't change behavior. `readFile` and `stat` are kept because they handle errors differently from the built-in ones.

### How?

Removed the `readlink` option.

Measured on our project (pnpm, Next 16.3, webpack build, `output: 'standalone'`):

- Running only `nodeFileTrace` with the same inputs: 17.3–18.1s → 12.1–12.9s, with an identical list of traced files
- "Collecting build traces" on CI (GitHub Actions, 2 vCPU): 42–57s → 26s
- `.nft.json` files and the standalone output are identical before and after the change

Fixes #100869

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: fix lost idle wakeup in the snapshot loop
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Fixes a race in the dev mode background snapshot loop that could sometimes get idle and busy periods confused. When that happens, idle snapshots are suppressed until the 300 s / 120 s fallback timers.

### Why?

The snapshot loop reacted to `idle_start_event` / `idle_end_event`, which use `Event::notify`. That only wakes listeners that are registered before notification. The loop re-created each listener after handling it, and treated the event kind as a statement about the current state:

1. turbo-tasks goes idle: idle-start notified (listener S1 ready)
2. goes busy: idle-end notified (listener E1 ready)
3. goes idle again: idle-start notified, but S1 was already notified, so this one reaches nobody
4. the loop handles S1 (arms the idle timer), then E1 (`idle_time = far_future()`)

turbo-tasks is now idle, but nothing re-arms the timer until the next transition. The mirror image (a stale idle-start handled while busy) arms the timer for a busy system. `active_time` drifts the same way.

### How?

The backend's `ActivityMonitor` (`backend/activity.rs`) publishes its activity through a `tokio::sync::watch` channel holding `BackendActivity::{Idle { since }, Busy, Stopping}`. Replacing the `Event`s. A watch receiver always sees the latest published value, so no change can be lost; changes can only be coalesced. Because an idle value carries the time its idle period began, a coalesced idle → busy → idle still shows up as a new value.

prs.title: Add instrumentationInject for adapter-supplied instrumentation
prs.author: kakadiadarpan
prs.body:
### What?

Adds an `instrumentationInject?: string[]` config option. Next.js compiles one module that runs every entry's `register` and `onRequestError`, then the project's own `instrumentation.{ts,js}` if it has one. This works like `instrumentationClientInject` does for the client.

```ts
// set by a deployment adapter in modifyConfig, or a config wrapper like withSentry
config.instrumentationInject ??= []
config.instrumentationInject.push('./path/to/instrumentation.js')
```

```text
instrumentation slot
  → each instrumentationInject entry, in array order
  → then the project's instrumentation file, if there is one
```

### Why?

Hosting platforms want to give every app default instrumentation, such as OpenTelemetry tracing. Today that means asking users to add an `instrumentation.ts` and a dependency to their project. This hook lets an adapter or a config wrapper supply the module at build time instead. The user's files, `package.json` and lockfile stay untouched, and Next.js installs nothing.

### How?

- Anyone can set the field: a deployment adapter in `modifyConfig`, or a config wrapper such as `withSentry`. Whoever sets it decides whether to inject when the project already has its own instrumentation file.
- Both bundlers generate the same CommonJS module: it requires every entry from the project root, then the project's instrumentation file, and passes them to `combineInstrumentation` (`next/dist/lib/combine-instrumentation`).

prs.title: server actions: read cache kinds lazily
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What?

The server actions transform now reads the known custom cache kinds lazily, the same way it already reads the hash salt (#100950). Editing the cache handler config no longer invalidates every module's analysis: only modules that use `"use cache: <kind>"` with a custom kind depend on it.

## Why?

Turbopack read the cache kinds unconditionally for every JS module it parsed, but the transform only needs them to validate `"use cache: <kind>"`. A plain `"use cache"` returns before that check, and most modules have no directives at all. Every module therefore depended on a value it almost never uses, and the whole set was cloned for every module.

## How?

- **Generic lazy config value.** `HashSalt` from #100950 becomes `LazyValue<T>`, shared by `hash_salt` and `cache_kinds`. It's an enum: a plain value, or a provider implementing the one-method `LazyGet<T>` trait (`fn get(&self) -> &T`), both behind an `Arc` so cloning the config stays cheap. The transform only calls `get()` at the point of use, and borrows the value instead of copying it. It deserializes from the plain value, so the webpack options (`hashSalt`, `cacheKinds`) are unchanged. `Debug` never prints the contents, because the salt can be the encryption key. `next-custom-transforms` doesn't depend on `turbo-tasks` (it's also built for webpack and wasm), which is why the provider is a trait rather than a `LazyReadRef` variant.
- **Turbopack.** `NextServerActions` reads both cells with `Vc::lazy_reader()` (#1010
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: only read conditionally needed values where they are used
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What?

Two tasks now await values they need only in one branch inside that branch, so they no longer depend on those values otherwise. Output doesn't change.

- **Client reference manifest** (`next-core`, `build_manifest`): the asset suffix (e.g. `?dpl=<id>`) is read only when the deployment id is *not* appended at runtime. When it is appended at runtime, a new deployment id no longer re-runs `build_manifest` for every App endpoint. That task walks all client references and chunks.
- **Resolve result processing** (`turbopack`, `process_resolve_result`): `import_externals` from the module options context is read only when an `External` result is replaced. Other resolve results no longer read the options context for it.

## Why?

Found by scanning for reads that happen unconditionally but are only used conditionally. Each one gave the task a dependency it usually doesn't use, so unrelated changes re-ran it. These two need no `lazy_reader()`: the decision is made in async code, so the await can simply move into the branch.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p turbopack`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` for `turbopack`, `next-core`
- No new tests: the changes only move awaits, and existing tests and CI cover the behavior.

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: keep recorded GC roots until their TTL expires
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

With Turbopack GC enabled, a task recorded in the persisted GC roots map now stays protected from collection until its TTL expires. Before, a recorded root was dropped from the map as soon as it became resident again. This also fixes pinned roots falling out of the roots map after their `Meta` was evicted.

### Why?

At refresh time, `gc_roots_refresh_and_age_out` dropped every *resident* root from the persisted roots map, assuming the pass's root scan would judge it. But the judgement would ~always judge them as dead.  A task becomes a root because it had only transient pins from a prior session, if we read it back to 'refresh' then it doens't have those transient pins and will always be collected.  On a warm `next dev` start, startup invalidation propagates through the aggregation graph and restores almost every prior root before anything requests it. So every root that hadn't been re-pinned yet was collected in the first GC pass, along with its whole exclusive subtree. The 3-day TTL never applied, and the next session had to recompute and re-persist everything.

On `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages` with GC enabled:
- a warm session that idled before its first request collected about 4.3M tasks;
- the next session then ran as slowly as a cold one.

A related bug: the root scan can't see a task whose `Meta` has been evicted, so the refresh also dropped roots that were still pinned.

### How?

**Once a root, always a root, until it ages out.**

prs.title: turbopack-node: linear IPC frame parsing with eager UTF-8 decoding
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

The Turbopack Node.js child-process IPC receiver now frames length-prefixed packets in linear time and decodes each payload to a UTF-8 string as it reads it. The logic lives in a side-effect-free `PacketReader` class with unit tests.

### Why?

The old receiver concatenated its entire buffered input on every socket `data` event. A large packet that arrived in many chunks was copied repeatedly, which is quadratic.

Queued packets also held onto received Buffer views. Decoding each payload as soon as it is complete means the queue holds independent strings, and payload chunks never have to be assembled into an intermediate Buffer.  Plus string concatenation is generally quite fast.

The wire protocol, transport and child lifecycle are unchanged.

prs.title: Keep loaded config from sharing objects with defaults and callers
prs.author: jamiboym
prs.body:
## Summary

`loadConfig` normalizes nested config objects in place (for example `images.localPatterns`, `images.path` with `basePath`, `experimental.staleTimes`). Some of those objects were not owned by the config being built:

- When a project's config omits `images` or `experimental.staleTimes`, the merged config used the module-level defaults (`imageConfigDefault`, `defaultConfig.experimental.staleTimes`) by reference. Normalization wrote into them, so a second config loaded in the same process inherited the first one's values.
